 Local governments concerned that property tax limit amendment could lessen services
 The constitutional amendment, which will appear on all North Carolina voters’ ballots, would limit increases in the total amount of property tax local governments can collect. 
 James O’Hara , Senior Writer 
 • 
 October 22, 2026 
 Dana Gentry Rogers Road is a neighborhood off of Eubanks Road. 
 On Nov. 3, North Carolina voters will be asked to decide on a constitutional amendment to require limits on property tax increases by local governments, possibly affecting services in Orange County, Chapel Hill and Carrboro.
 The amendment would require the N.C. General Assembly to enact a law limiting increases in the total amount of property tax local governments can collect. The amendment does not specify what the limit might be or establish a timeline for its implementation.
 An analysis by the North Carolina Housing Coalition estimated a levy limit allowing 2 percent growth above revenue-neutral collection would have reduced local government property tax revenue by more than $950 million statewide in each governing body’s last reevaluation year.
 The analysis estimated the average N.C. homeowner would have saved $84 annually, or $7 per month.
 “Is $7 off a homeowner’s tax bill worth losing Medicaid, is it worth losing SNAP assistance, is it worth losing public schools,” Rep. Allen Buansi (D-Orange) said. “That’s the kind of thing that folks must think about at the ballot.”
 Orange County is already facing budget pressures that could be worsened by restrictions on property tax revenue.
 Property taxes account for about 71 percent or $231 million of the County’s budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year.
 The County faced a gap of $21 million between projected revenues and expenditures at the beginning of its last budget process.
 Orange County Commissioner Amy Fowler said the County is facing increasing costs from inflation, new construction projects and federal policies that shift expenses for programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to local governments.
 If property tax revenue cannot keep up with these expenses, the county may have to consider reducing funding for its non-required services, Fowler said.
 “I want [voters] to realize it impacts local control and ability to help provide the things that they like and depend on, like schools and law enforcement and libraries and parks and even senior services,” she said.
 Rep. Julia Howard (R-Davie, Rowan, Yadkin), a primary sponsor of the amendment, said she supports it because the escalation of property taxes has been difficult for homeowners and that homeowners deserve predictable taxes each year.
 “Property tax collection should generally grow in line with inflation and population, and not simply because local government maybe wants to spend more money,” Howard said.
 Buansi said the General Assembly can already pass a law limiting property tax increases by local governments and does not require an amendment.
 “I also suspect that another reason for this amendment being put forward is as a way for some people to say that they’re doing something without actually having done anything through the amendment itself,” he said.
 Fowler said there are a lot of unknowns the General Assembly did not clarify before putting the amendment on the ballot.
 “We don’t even know exactly what the levy limit will be, and so therefore what the consequences will be,” she said.
 Carrboro Town Council member Jason Merrill said a levy limit could have the unintended consequence of encouraging municipalities to raise taxes the maximum allowable amount to prepare for unexpected future expenses.
 “What I would expect decision makers in the future to land on that is we are going to go to the limit every single time just in case,” Merrill said.
 The amendment could also affect Chapel Hill and Carrboro, which rely on property taxes to fund services like street maintenance, public safety, trash collection services and public parks.
 The Housing Coalition’s analysis found that Carrboro would have collected 16 percent less property tax revenue under the hypothetical limit. Chapel Hill would have collected 10 percent less.
 Merrill said Carrboro approved a significant property tax hike as part of its 2025-26 budget to address a budget shortfall. He said Carrboro raised taxes to maintain current services, not to fund additional ones.
 “You don’t realize how much gets done until it stops getting done,” Merrill said. “So I think it’s critical to allow the people at the local level who are most affected by it to have the authority to make decisions about what services they need and want.”
